SQLLineage comes to the rescue. Given a SQL command, SQLLineage will tell you its 15 source and target tables, without worrying about Tokens, Keyword, Identifier and all the jagons used by SQL parsers. 16 17 Behind the scene, SQLLineage pluggable leverages parser library ([`sqlfluff`](https://github.com/sqlfluff/sqlfluff) 18 and [`sqlparse`](https://github.com/andialbrecht/sqlparse)) to parse the SQL command, analyze the AST, stores the lineage 19 information in a graph (using graph library [`networkx`](https://github.com/networkx/networkx)), and brings you all the 20 human-readable result with ease. 21 22 ## Demo & Documentation 23 Talk is cheap, show me a [demo](https://reata.github.io/sqllineage/). 24 25 [Documentation](https://sqllineage.readthedocs.io) is online hosted by readthedocs, and you can check the 26 [release note](https://sqllineage.readthedocs.io/en/latest/release_note/changelog.html) there. 27 28 29 ## Quick Start 30 Install sqllineage via PyPI: 31 ```bash 32 $ pip install sqllineage 33 ``` 34 35 Using sqllineage command to parse a quoted-query-string: 36 ``` 37 $ sqllineage -e "insert into db1.table1 select * from db2.table2" 38 Statements(#): 1 39 Source Tables: 40 db2.table2 41 Target Tables: 42 db1.table1 43 ``` 44 45 Or you can parse a SQL file with -f option: 46 ``` 47 $ sqllineage -f foo.sql 48 Statements(#): 1 49 Source Tables: 50 db1.table_foo 51 db1.table_bar 52 Target Tables: 53 db2.table_baz 54 ``` 55 56 ## Advanced Usage 57 58 ### Multiple SQL Statements 59 Lineage is combined from multiple SQL statements, with intermediate tables identified: 60 ``` 61 $ sqllineage -e "insert into db1.table1 select * from db2.table2; insert into db3.table3 select * from db1.table1;" 62 Statements(#): 2 63 Source Tables: 64 db2.table2 65 Target Tables: 66 db3.table3 67 Intermediate Tables: 68 db1.table1 69 ``` 70 71 ### Verbose Lineage Result 72 And if you want to see lineage for each SQL statement, just toggle verbose option 73 ``` 74 $ sqllineage -v -e "insert into db1.table1 select * from db2.table2; insert into db3.table3 select * from db1.table1;" 75 Statement #1: insert into db1.table1 select * from db2.table2; 76 table read: [Table: db2.table2] 77 table write: [Table: db1.table1] 78 table cte: [] 79 table rename: [] 80 table drop: [] 81 Statement #2: insert into db3.table3 select * from db1.table1; 82 table read: [Table: db1.table1] 83 table write: [Table: db3.table3] 84 table cte: [] 85 table rename: [] 86 table drop: [] 87 ========== 88 Summary: 89 Statements(#): 2 90 Source Tables: 91 db2.table2 92 Target Tables: 93 db3.table3 94 Intermediate Tables: 95 db1.table1 96 ``` 97 98 ### Dialect-Awareness Lineage 99 By default, sqllineage use `ansi` dialect to parse and validate your SQL. However, some SQL syntax you take for granted 100 in daily life might not be in ANSI standard. In addition, different SQL dialects have different set of SQL keywords, 101 further weakening sqllineage's capabilities when keyword used as table name or column name. To get the most out of 102 sqllineage, we strongly encourage you to pass the dialect to assist the lineage analyzing. 103 104 Take below example, `INSERT OVERWRITE` statement is only supported by big data solutions like Hive/SparkSQL, and `MAP` 105 is a reserved keyword in Hive thus can not be used as table name while it is not for SparkSQL. Both ansi and hive dialect 106 tell you this causes syntax error and sparksql gives the correct result: 107 ``` 108 $ sqllineage -e "INSERT OVERWRITE TABLE map SELECT * FROM foo" 109 ... 110 sqllineage.exceptions.InvalidSyntaxException: This SQL statement is unparsable, please check potential syntax error for SQL 111 112 $ sqllineage -e "INSERT OVERWRITE TABLE map SELECT * FROM foo" --dialect=hive 113 ... 114 sqllineage.exceptions.InvalidSyntaxException: This SQL statement is unparsable, please check potential syntax error for SQL 115 116 $ sqllineage -e "INSERT OVERWRITE TABLE map SELECT * FROM foo" --dialect=sparksql 117 Statements(#): 1 118 Source Tables: 119 .foo 120 Target Tables: 121 .map 122 ``` 123 124 Use `sqllineage --dialects` to see all available dialects. 125 126 ### Column-Level Lineage 127 We also support column level lineage in command line interface, set level option to column, all column lineage path will 128 be printed. 129 130 ```sql 131 INSERT INTO foo 132 SELECT a.col1, 133 b.col1 AS col2, 134 c.col3_sum AS col3, 135 col4, 136 d.* 137 FROM bar a 138 JOIN baz b 139 ON a.id = b.bar_id 140 LEFT JOIN (SELECT bar_id, sum(col3) AS col3_sum 141 FROM qux 142 GROUP BY bar_id) c 143 ON a.id = sq.bar_id 144 CROSS JOIN quux d; 145 146 INSERT INTO corge 147 SELECT a.col1, 148 a.col2 + b.col2 AS col2 149 FROM foo a 150 LEFT JOIN grault b 151 ON a.col1 = b.col1; 152 ``` 153 154 Suppose this sql is stored in a file called test.sql 155 156 ``` 157 $ sqllineage -f test.sql -l column 158 .corge.col1 <- .foo.col1 <- .bar.col1 159 .corge.col2 <- .foo.col2 <- .baz.col1 160 .corge.col2 <- .grault.col2 161 .foo.* <- .quux.* 162 .foo.col3 <- c.col3_sum <- .qux.col3 163 .foo.col4 <- col4 164 ``` 165 166 ### MetaData-Awareness Lineage 167 By observing the column lineage generated from previous step, you'll possibly notice that: 168 1. `.foo.* <- .quux.*`: the wildcard is not expanded. 169 2. `.foo.col4 <- col4`: col4 is not assigned with source table. 170 171 It's not perfect because we don't know the columns encoded in `*` of table `quux`. The problem is about **column-level lineage parsing for INSERT statements**:

1. **Current behavior**: When parsing `"insert into target select user_id, user_name from source"`, the column lineage shows target columns as `user_id`, `user_name` (taken from the SELECT clause)
